## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why2: Approvals, reviews, procurement and switching are everyday words when I sell to hotel groups, and the question is plain on first reading.
screens.why3: I sell the pilots myself, so I know a data protection review, the PMS check and a one-hotel trial are what stand in the way.
screens.why4: The hint's four examples cover the real kinds of friction without limiting my answer, and leaving this out of the study is a fair escape.
screens.why5: The data protection review is my wording, but I listed three items without ranking them, so 'slows the purchase most' adds a claim I did not make and drops the other two.
screens.instead: What could slow down or stop a purchase? Keep the box and hint, and write the belief as: 'A data protection review of guest calls can slow or stop the purchase.'

screens.why1: Right after I named what could slow a purchase, it makes sense for Keel to show me the belief it drew from that before testing it.
screens.why2: Data protection review, PMS and works council are all everyday words for someone selling to German hotel groups, and the belief is one short sentence.
screens.why3: I hit these hurdles when selling to hotel groups, and guest calls carrying card and personal data make the data protection review a belief I can judge.
screens.why4: The three rows are distinct and believable for Germany, but 'call monitoring' is slightly off because our AI answers missed calls rather than monitoring staff, so a works council would care more about call recording.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my data protection review of guest calls as the main hurdle and adds only the claim that it slows the purchase most, which is what I saved.
screens.instead: Keep the belief and change the third row to 'Works council sign-off on recording calls'.

screens.why1: Right after I named what could slow a purchase and checked Keel's wording, it is obvious why I now pick the one friction to test before moving on from the commercial beliefs.
screens.why2: The options are plain in my trade (PMS, works council, data protection review), but the bar's "last time" does not say last time of what, and I have to read it twice to see it means the group's last software purchase.
screens.why3: I sell to German hotel groups and hear about guest-call data, PMS checks and works councils on my sales calls, so I can pick from what I know, though no one has yet proved which slows a deal most.
screens.why4: The three are distinct, real German hotel-group hurdles and include my own answer, but "our PMS" slips into the buyer's voice on a screen addressed to me, and the owner's approval or a change to call forwarding are not offered.
screens.why5: "A data protection review of guest calls" is my wording, but Keel adds "slows the purchase most", and its bar only tests whether the review was needed and took long, never whether it was the biggest hurdle.
screens.instead: Which one do you believe slows a hotel group's purchase most? A data protection review of guest calls / A check that bookings land in the group's PMS / Works council sign-off on call monitoring -- Holds if at least 2 in 3 say that, the last time their group bought software that touches guest calls, this review was needed and took a long time.

screens.why1: After who decides, what it costs and what could stop a purchase, it is obvious to ask what first real commitment I want, and my pilot is exactly that step.
screens.why2: "First real step" with the hint about time, data, money or a signature is plain on first reading, and I can answer it straight away in my own words.
screens.why3: I sell this pilot every week and set its terms myself, so I can answer from what I actually do.
screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip, and "Leave this out of the study" fits a founder who has no step to test, while the open box takes my answer as typed.
screens.why5: My step is kept word for word, but Keel's belief says most reservation agents would pay €3,000, when I named the revenue director as the one who decides and an agent never pays for a pilot.
screens.instead: Question: "What's the first real step you'd want the hotel group's revenue director to take?" Belief: "Most hotel group revenue directors would pay €3,000 now for a money-back pilot at one hotel."

screens.why1: Right after I named the first real step, it makes sense for Keel to show the commitment belief and bar it will test as the last commercial check.
screens.why2: "Money-back pilot at one hotel" is how I sell it, and the "no more than 1 in 3" bar reads clearly the first time.
screens.why3: I know the €3,000 pilot and how it sells, but this asks me to judge what reservation agents would pay when they never see or sign that spend, so I could only guess.
screens.why4: The screen shows a belief and bar to check, with no options, rows, chips or value box.
screens.why5: My pilot terms and price are kept, but the payer is wrong: I sell to the hotel group's revenue director with the owner's agreement, so reservation agents would not pay €3,000.
screens.instead: Most hotel group revenue directors would pay €3,000 now for a money-back pilot at one hotel; holds if no more than 1 in 3 say probably not or no.

screens.why1: An opt-in for interested respondents makes sense just before the study goes out, but I named my €3,000 pilot as the first step only two screens ago, so asking again without linking the two feels abrupt.
screens.why2: "Pilot" is my everyday word and the hint is short, but I need a second read to tell whether this means my paid, money-back pilot or just a free list of people who are interested.
screens.why3: I sell a pilot at one hotel, so I know straight away whether I want respondents to be able to ask for one.
screens.why4: The screen shows no options, rows, chips or value box, only an optional offer and Continue.
screens.why5: The word "pilot" is mine, but the screen drops what I typed about it: €3,000 up front, one hotel, up to 8 weeks and money back.
screens.instead: Do you want people who answer to be able to ask about your pilot (€3,000 money-back, one hotel, up to 8 weeks)? Optional, and it does not change their answers.

screens.why1: As the last step before strangers see my study, it makes obvious sense to choose who puts the questions to them.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but "This account runs on its own AI" and "Keel's credits" need a second read, because they don't say what I would have to do or pay to get the interviewer.
screens.why3: I know my own study and my reservation agents and directors, who take calls all day and can be reached by a tappable form or a voice, so I can decide this from what I know.
screens.why4: The faces and the read-and-tap route are distinct choices, but a preselected face that is locked on this account makes it feel less like a real choice, and nothing says what unlocks it beyond credits.
screens.why5: The screen rewrites nothing I typed about Codyco, the hotels or the calls, and only asks how the questions are delivered.
screens.instead: Who should ask your questions? Options: "People read and tap (included on your plan)" or "An AI interviewer speaks them (needs Keel credits)".
